title: U-331 sinks HMS Barham

facts.text: On the afternoon of 25 November 1941, the U-boat U-331 under Oberleutnant zur See Hans-Diedrich von Tiesenhausen, 28, heard the engines of the British Mediterranean Fleet's battleships off the Egyptian coast and moved to intercept.
A week earlier, on 17 November, the same boat had landed eight commandos on the Egyptian coast to blow up a railway line. They failed.
At 16:18 a sonar operator on the destroyer HMS Jervis picked up U-331 about 1,000 yards away but dismissed the contact. The U-boat slipped through the destroyer screen.
At 16:25 Tiesenhausen fired four bow torpedoes at about 375 meters, a very short range for a battleship target. Three of them struck HMS Barham on her port side, almost together.

Right after firing, U-331's conning tower broke the surface, probably thrown up by the bow wave of the battleship Valiant close by. She was fired on, then plunged out of control to about 265 meters, far below her rated depth of 150 meters. She survived undamaged, and the escorts never attacked her.
Barham rolled over to port. About four minutes after the torpedoes hit, her after magazines exploded and she sank.
Of the 1,311 men aboard, 862 died, among them her captain, Geoffrey Cooke. About 450 were rescued.
Tiesenhausen could not see what he had done. He radioed only that he had hit a Queen Elizabeth class battleship, and the Germans could not confirm a sinking.

The British kept the loss secret for two months. Next of kin were told weeks later and asked to say nothing, and the Admiralty announced it only on 27 January 1942. Tiesenhausen received the Knight's Cross that same day.
A year later, on 17 November 1942, aircraft from HMS Formidable sank U-331 off Algiers after she had signaled surrender. 32 men died; Tiesenhausen was among 17 survivors.

He spent the rest of the war as a prisoner in Britain and Canada, went back to Canada in 1951, and lived near Vancouver as an interior designer and nature photographer until his death in 2000, aged 87.

declassified.fact: While the loss was still hidden, the Scottish medium Helen Duncan claimed to have contacted the spirit of a Barham sailor, and so came to the authorities' attention. She is remembered as the last person jailed under Britain's Witchcraft Act of 1735.

body:
A U-boat slipped through the destroyer screen, fired four torpedoes from 375 meters, then broke the surface right beside the British fleet.

It dove out of control to about 265 meters, far below its rated depth of 150, and survived.

25 November 1941. U-331, under Oberleutnant zur See Hans-Diedrich von Tiesenhausen, 28, found the Mediterranean Fleet's battleships off the Egyptian coast. A sonar contact on HMS Jervis was dismissed. At 16:25 three torpedoes struck HMS Barham on her port side. She rolled over, and about four minutes later her after magazines exploded. 862 of the 1,311 men aboard died.

Tiesenhausen could report only a hit. The Admiralty announced the loss on 27 January 1942, and he received the Knight's Cross that same day.
